questions.q: According to this lesson, which statement best describes why most large enterprises run a hybrid architecture?
options: Cloud providers require every enterprise customer to keep at least one on-premises data center under contract
Hybrid is typically a certification requirement rather than an architectural outcome
It is usually the result of several independent forces — legacy systems, data residency, M&A, and gradual migration — not a single deliberate day-one strategy
Public cloud platforms cannot legally host regulated workloads under any circumstances
questions.explain: The lesson identifies four real, independent forces that push enterprises toward hybrid; it is almost never a clean strategic choice made from a blank slate.

questions.q: Why do some legacy systems stay on-premises indefinitely rather than getting migrated?
options: The cost, risk, and lack of a clear cloud-native replacement often mean the migration business case doesn't hold up on its own merits
On-premises hardware is always cheaper to operate than any cloud equivalent
Cloud providers refuse to support any workload older than five years
Legacy systems are technically incapable of being virtualized under any circumstances
questions.explain: A positive migration ROI isn't guaranteed just because a migration project exists — for high-risk, poorly understood legacy systems, the business case frequently fails on its own terms.

questions.q: Which scenario in this lesson illustrates hybrid architecture arriving as an unavoidable consequence rather than a planned decision?
options: A team choosing a multi-region deployment for disaster recovery
A company acquiring another organization and immediately inheriting its data centers, Active Directory forest, and in-progress cloud migration
An architect selecting a service mesh for a Kubernetes cluster
A developer choosing a managed database over a self-hosted one
questions.explain: M&A forces two independently-evolved IT estates together on a timeline set by legal and finance, producing an immediate hybrid environment with no architectural decision involved.

questions.q: Why can data residency and latency requirements keep a workload on-premises permanently, rather than just until the cloud matures further?
options: They are legal and physical constraints — jurisdictional data rules and round-trip latency — that cloud maturity or cost improvements don't resolve
Cloud regions cannot be added fast enough to keep up with enterprise demand
Data residency rules apply only to workloads under 1 terabyte in size
Latency-sensitive workloads are always migrated first in a cloud adoption plan
questions.explain: Data residency is a legal/jurisdictional constraint and latency is a physics constraint; neither is solved by the cloud simply becoming more capable or cheaper over time.

questions.q: Why does a phased, multi-year migration plan often produce a long-lived hybrid state instead of a short transitional one?
options: Phased migrations are illegal in regulated industries
Cloud contracts require a minimum multi-year hybrid period before full migration is permitted
Phased migrations always complete faster than planned, so hybrid periods are typically brief
Budget cycles, staffing limits, and large application portfolios routinely extend the 'in progress' period far beyond the original plan
questions.explain: Large enterprise migrations are executed in waves over years; real-world constraints like budget and staffing frequently stretch that timeline well past what was originally planned, making the 'temporary' hybrid state durable.
